title: Classification / Odd One Out — In-Depth Guide — Part 14 of 16

questions.question: What does 'Classification by Relation' test?
options: Whether a group of item PAIRS share a common relationship, with one pair having a different underlying relationship
questions.rationale: This tests whether a group of paired items shares a common relationship (like part-whole or cause-effect), identifying the pair with a different relationship.

questions.question: What does 'Pair Classification' specifically test?
options: Whether a set of item pairs are all connected by the same type of relationship, with one pair breaking that pattern
questions.rationale: Pair classification looks at pairs of items (not single items) and tests whether they all share the same connecting relationship, finding the pair that doesn't.

questions.question: What is a 'Pair-Relation Vector'?
options: A vector describing a single item only
A representation of the specific relationship connecting a pair of items, similar to a relationship vector in analogy
A vector with no relational meaning
questions.rationale: This represents the specific relationship connecting a given pair of items, paralleling the relationship vector concept used in analogy reasoning.

questions.question: What do 'Common Pair Relationships' likely catalog?
options: A reference of frequently-tested pair relationship types (part-whole, cause-effect, etc.) relevant to pair classification
questions.rationale: This catalogs the commonly-tested types of pair relationships, providing a quick reference for recognizing which relationship type connects a given set of pairs.

questions.question: What is the key difference between 'Classification' and 'Analogy'?
options: Classification finds the one item that breaks a shared group property; analogy finds a new pair that matches a given pair's relationship
questions.rationale: Classification identifies the outlier that breaks a shared property among a group, while analogy matches a relationship from a given pair onto a new pair — related but distinct skills.

questions.question: What is the key difference between 'Classification' and 'Series'?
options: Classification finds a static group's outlier; series reasoning finds the next/missing term in an ordered sequence
questions.rationale: Classification deals with a static, unordered group and its odd one out, while series reasoning deals with an ordered sequence and predicting its next or missing term.

questions.question: What is the key difference between 'Classification' and 'Coding-Decoding'?
options: Classification finds the item breaking a shared property; coding-decoding finds a hidden transformation rule turning an input into an output
questions.rationale: Classification is about spotting a broken shared property within a group, while coding-decoding is about discovering and applying a hidden input-to-output transformation rule.

questions.question: What do 'Common Exam Traps' in classification likely consolidate?
options: A list unrelated to classification errors
The recurring mistake patterns (like the function-based and material-based traps) covered earlier in the lesson, gathered into one reference
questions.rationale: This consolidates the various trap patterns covered throughout the lesson into one convenient, quick-reference summary.

questions.question: What is 'The Three Supporters Rule'?
options: A rule requiring exactly three items in every group
A heuristic that a genuine shared property should be clearly supported by at least three of the items, not just one or two coincidentally
A rule that only applies to numbers
A rule with no practical use
questions.rationale: This heuristic suggests that a genuinely valid shared property should be clearly supported by several (at least three) items, reducing the risk of mistaking a coincidental pattern for the real rule.

questions.question: What does 'What If Two Items Look Different?' address?
options: A situation that never actually occurs
How to proceed when more than one item initially seems to be the exception, requiring further property analysis to disambiguate
A situation with no valid solution
questions.rationale: This addresses the common situation where two items both initially seem like possible exceptions, requiring deeper property analysis to determine which one is the true outlier.
